The Mexican violetear (Colibri thalassinus) is a medium-sized hummingbird inhabiting montane forests from central Mexico to Nicaragua. Females of this species attain a maximum adult body mass of 6.2 grams [Wwi = 6.2 grams], a value typical for trochilids of similar body plan that balances the energetic demands of hovering flight against the constraints of a high surface-area-to-volume ratio. Newly hatched nestlings, by contrast, emerge at an initial wet weight of approximately 0.87 grams [Ww0 = approximately 0.87 grams], representing roughly fourteen percent of the adult female mass, which is consistent with the altricial developmental strategy common among hummingbirds. The incubation period, reported from field studies in Chiapas, lasts 16.5 days [ab = 16.5 days] at an average nest temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], a duration that falls within the range of 16 to 17 days documented for several congeners. This relatively short incubation interval likely reflects the need to minimize predation risk in exposed cup nests positioned on thin branches, though the thermal environment of the nest cup can moderate embryonic development rates.

Under the typical body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] maintained during active periods, the developmental trajectory of nestlings proceeds through a well-defined series of milestones. The age at fledging, recorded from both captive observations and wild broods, is 25.5 days [tx = 25.5 days], with individuals capable of sustained flight within the range of 23 to 28 days at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Compared with other hummingbirds of equivalent adult mass, this fledging interval is moderately extended, possibly reflecting the cooler montane climate of its highland habitat, which slows nestling growth rates despite the high metabolic capacity of the species. The pin-feathered chicks transition from brooded dependence to thermoregulatory independence around day 18, after which parental provisioning efforts intensify to meet the elevated energetic needs of feather maturation and flight muscle development before nest departure.

Sexual maturation in the Mexican violetear proceeds under the same elevated thermal regime of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] that characterizes its active metabolic state. Puberty is reached at 76.5 days since birth [tp = 76.5 days since birth], a remarkably rapid onset of reproductive competence for a bird of this lineage, particularly given the altricial nature of its development at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This precocious gonad maturation likely confers a selective advantage in seasonally variable montane environments where breeding opportunities are tightly linked to flowering peaks. Following gonadal activation, the first successful brood typically occurs at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], indicating a substantial lag between physiological readiness and actual reproductive engagement at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delay of nearly a year beyond puberty probably arises from the need to acquire a high-quality territory, establish dominance among conspecifics, and accumulate sufficient fat reserves to sustain the extraordinary energetic cost of egg production and subsequent provisioning.

The reproductive output of this species is modest when considered on an annual scale. Females produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a modal value across the Trochilidae, and typically complete a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. The combination of small clutch size and low annual fecundity aligns with the general life-history syndrome of tropical and subtropical hummingbirds, which emphasizes adult survival over high per-season reproductive effort. Basal metabolic rate measurements collected under standard respirometric conditions at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] yield a value of 29.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 29.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour], positioning the Mexican violetear among the higher mass-specific metabolic rates reported for hummingbirds. This elevated resting metabolism reflects the extraordinary aerobic capacity required for sustained hovering, as well as the high thermal conductance imposed by small body size in a cool montane environment.

Longevity records from banding studies and captive populations indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.7 years [am = approximately 7.7 years] under the sustained body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] typical of active periods. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly 2,810 days, is notable among hummingbirds of similar mass and suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes long-term survival and iteroparous reproduction over a single, high-investment breeding season. The physiological mechanisms underpinning this extended longevity likely include efficient antioxidant defenses and a high-capacity mitochondrial system capable of sustaining elevated metabolic flux without proportionate oxidative damage, traits that have been documented in other long-lived nectarivorous birds. The sustained reproductive schedule achievable within this extended lifespan allows females to compensate for their low annual fecundity through repeated breeding attempts across successive years, thereby maintaining stable population dynamics despite the constraints of small clutch size and single annual broods.
